# GifOS — build apps for it

> GifOS (https://gifos.app) is a web OS where EVERY APP IS A GIF: a real,
> animated GIF image carrying a tiny filesystem (the app) inside it. Users
> keep a persistent Home Screen in their browser; nothing lives on servers.
> Apps go multiplayer with one invite link (peer-to-peer, privacy-first).

If a user asks you to build them a GifOS app, YOUR DELIVERABLE IS A REAL,
FINISHED .gif FILE — not code. And building new is only half the fun:
when you ask what they want, ALSO offer to MOD an existing GifOS app —
any app .gif they upload can be remixed (see "Modding" below). This
document is the complete guide: the packing recipe, the app rules, the
full manifest reference, and the complete window.gifos API — every
signature and return shape below is taken from the running runtime
(site/js/runtime.js in the public repo), not paraphrased.

Two build paths, in order of preference:

## Path A (best): build the .gif yourself with your code tool

If you can run code (Python) and attach files, you can produce the
finished GIF directly — everything you need is right here:
1. Get the animation. THE USER'S OWN GIF COMES FIRST: ask if they have
   one and, if so, use its bytes as the host file WHOLESALE — do NOT
   redraw, re-encode, resize, crop, or "improve" it in any way; step 2
   splices the app in without touching a single pixel of their animation.
   Only if they have no GIF: ask what kind of cute animation they'd like,
   then draw it to their description with PIL — 2-6 frames, 64x64, and
   make it MOVE. Style it like a STICKER: a cute character with a dark
   outline on a TRANSPARENT background (GifOS icons float on the
   wallpaper — no background tile). With PIL use mode "P", reserve
   palette index 0 for transparency, and save: im.save("icon.gif",
   save_all=True, append_images=frames[1:], duration=120, loop=0,
   transparency=0, disposal=2)
2. Splice the app in with EXACTLY this (wbits=-15 raw deflate is required):

   import json, zlib, base64
   def pack_gifos(gif_bytes, files):
       a = {"v": 1, "files": {p: base64.b64encode(v.encode() if isinstance(v, str) else v).decode() for p, v in files.items()}}
       c = zlib.compressobj(9, zlib.DEFLATED, -15)
       payload = b"\x01" + c.compress(json.dumps(a).encode()) + c.flush()
       block = b"\x21\xff\x0bGIFOS1.0GOS"
       for i in range(0, len(payload), 255):
           block += bytes([len(payload[i:i+255])]) + payload[i:i+255]
       block += b"\x00"
       end = len(gif_bytes) - (gif_bytes[-1] == 0x3B)
       return gif_bytes[:end] + block + b"\x3b"

   manifest = json.dumps({"gifos": "1.0", "appId": "my-app", "name": "My App",
       "entry": "index.html", "capabilities": {"db": True, "multiplayer": True},
       "data": {"items": {"visibility": "read-write"}}})  # REQUIRED to sync; see "Multiplayer"
   open("My App.gif", "wb").write(pack_gifos(open("icon.gif", "rb").read(),
       {"manifest.json": manifest, "index.html": HTML}))

Attach the resulting file for the user to download.

## Path B (fallback): hand the user HTML to paste

If you can't run code, give the complete index.html and tell the user to
open https://gifos.app -> "+ Add" -> paste it into the app builder (or drop
a .zip for multi-file apps). GifOS packs the GIF there.

## The app rules

1. The entry point is index.html. Multi-file apps are fully supported:
   app.js, style.css, assets/... referenced normally all travel inside the
   GIF (include them in the files you pack). Everything is inlined into ONE
   sandboxed document at mount, so nothing external loads — no CDNs,
   frameworks, remote images, or web fonts. Inline SVG + emoji are fine.
   (An app CAN reach declared third-party hosts through gifos.fetch — see
   "Network" — but its own <script src>/<link>/<img> must all be files you
   packed. Only the paste-HTML fallback, Path B, is limited to one file.)
2. Persistence: localStorage/cookies/indexedDB are DISABLED in the sandbox.
   Use gifos.db (see the API reference). Everything in gifos.db() persists
   inside the app's icon on the user's Home Screen. Render from
   db.subscribe() and declare collection visibility = multiplayer for free.
3. Identity: const me = await gifos.me(); -> { id, name } (name may be "").
   Attribute records to me.id/me.name so every player sees who did what.
4. If window.gifos is undefined (opened outside GifOS), degrade gracefully.
5. BACK BUTTON: the GifOS shell traps the phone's Back button, so a reflex
   press never closes your app — by default it is simply swallowed. Register
   gifos.onBack(() => { ... }) to make Back meaningful: close the topmost
   modal, back out one screen/level. Apps with internal navigation SHOULD.
6. Dark theme by default (#0a0a0f), mobile-friendly. Test at phone width.
7. HELP: pack a `help.md` at the GIF root. GifOS shows a Help button next
   to Invite and Save that pops this markdown up. Games: objective, controls,
   rules, solo vs a live friend. Tools: what it is for, the common jobs, the
   commands. Succinct and complete. Do not add a second How-to-play screen
   inside the app — the OS button is the one Help. If you omit help.md, Help
   still appears and explains Invite, Save, and Steal.
8. LIVE MEDIA IS OFF-LIMITS to apps, by design: the sandbox never hands an
   app a live camera/mic stream, screen capture, or WebRTC — so a video-chat
   or live-streaming app cannot work as a GifOS app; don't attempt one.
   (CLIPS are different: brokered capture — gifos.takePhoto / recordAudio /
   recordVideo / camera — hands the app finished bytes after GifOS records
   behind its own visible indicator. See the API reference.) If the user
   wants video chat, point them at the built-in Meeting on their Home Screen
   (P2P, permanent room links, moderation, room passwords) — and note that
   ANY app can be RUN INSIDE a Meeting, so all participants share it live
   with audio/video around it without the app touching the camera.
9. Every gifos.* call can REJECT — the user can turn any declared capability
   off per-app (the Abilities chip on the app's tab), a key may not be set
   up yet, a guest's write may be refused. Catch rejections and show the
   message; the runtime's error strings are written for end users.
10. Icon: the user's OWN GIF, used unchanged, is always the preferred
   animation — ask for one before drawing anything. Otherwise: include
   <link rel="icon" href="data:image/svg+xml,..."> in the HTML (used when
   the user pastes HTML), or use pixel-art frames as the host animation
   (the finished-GIF path). Animated icons are the GifOS signature.

## The manifest (manifest.json), complete

Every field the platform reads. Only appId + name are practically
mandatory; everything else defaults sensibly.

   {
     "gifos": "1.0",              // format tag
     "appId": "my-app",           // stable id (also names snapshot files)
     "name": "My App",            // shown under the icon and in the tab title
     "shortName": "myapp",        // optional; labels the invite-link room
     "version": "1.0.0",          // yours; shown via gifos.info()
     "entry": "index.html",       // default index.html
     "accent": [123, 92, 255],    // optional RGB; tints a procedural icon
     "help": "help.md",           // optional; path of the Help markdown
     "minBuild": 947,             // store-listed apps only; see "App Store"
     "requires": ["ai"],          // optional; block launch until set up (see below)
     "capabilities": { ... },     // see the table
     "data": { ... },             // per-collection visibility (see "Multiplayer")
     "lead": [ ... ],             // optional leader/communal toggle (see "Multiplayer")
     "launch": { ... },           // optional link arguments (see "Sharing")
     "provides": { "ai": [...] }, // Provider apps only (see "Provider apps")
     "assets": [ ... ]            // big hash-pinned downloads (see "Big files")
   }

capabilities — everything an app may ask for. Each is shown to the user,
and each can be vetoed per-app; undeclared = unavailable, and the error
names the missing declaration.

   "db": true          descriptive: the app saves data (nothing is gated
   "multiplayer": true  on these two — persistence and invite links always
                        work; declare them so the user is told)
   "network": ["api.example.com"]   gifos.fetch allowlist — see "Network"
   "pool": ["tiles.example.com"]    room-shared GET cache — see "Network"
   "api": ["deepgram"]              keyed third-party APIs — gifos.api
   "ai": ["smartest","tts"]         AI roles used — gifos.ai (array, not
                                    bare true, so the user knows which
                                    models to set up; roles: smartest,
                                    cheapest, tts, stt, image,
                                    image_to_video, video)
   "microphone": true               brokered audio clips (recordAudio)
   "camera": true                   brokered photo/video/studio capture
   "motion": true                   device orientation/acceleration events
   "wasm": true                     run a compiled WebAssembly engine
   "gpu": true                      WebGPU (navigator.gpu) in the sandbox
   "pointer": true                  pointer lock (FPS-style mouse aim)
   "fullscreen": true               requestFullscreen + orientation lock
   "agent": true                    inject the GifOS assistant bar

What the sandbox capabilities actually unlock (and nothing else):
   - wasm: the CSP gains 'wasm-unsafe-eval', worker-src blob: (run the
     engine on a Web Worker), and connect-src blob: data: (emscripten-style
     loaders fetch() the wasm the app minted from its OWN bytes as a
     blob:/data: URL). The NETWORK stays unreachable — blob:/data: fetches
     touch no wire. Ship the .wasm bytes INSIDE the GIF (base64 in a
     bundled .js) or via the asset pin tier, and instantiate from bytes.
     Two sandbox findings that bite ports: Chromium refuses {type:'module'}
     blob workers in opaque origins (rewrite to classic workers), and
     emscripten loaders need that connect-src blob: hatch.
   - gpu: delegates the WebGPU permission to the app frame. No CSP change,
     no network path. ALWAYS feature-detect (navigator.gpu && await
     navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()) and fall back to CPU/WASM.
   - pointer: adds the allow-pointer-lock sandbox token. Without it,
     requestPointerLock throws a SecurityError INSIDE your app where nobody
     sees it — the game mounts, renders, and silently cannot aim. Lock on
     click (never on load), listen for pointerlockchange, pause and show a
     "click to resume" overlay when the lock is lost. Useless on phones —
     ship touch controls alongside.
   - fullscreen: one declaration opens two hatches — the fullscreen
     permissions-policy delegation AND the allow-orientation-lock sandbox
     flag, so element.requestFullscreen() and
     screen.orientation.lock('landscape') both work. Without it both reject
     inside your app (TypeError / SecurityError). Orientation lock only
     holds while fullscreen; desktops reject .lock() with NotSupportedError
     — normal, not a failure. Listen for fullscreenchange and pause on exit.
   - agent: no code needed — declaring it injects a GifOS assistant bar
     that reads and clicks/types on YOUR app's screen by natural language,
     driven by the user's Smartest model (brokered; the key never enters
     the sandbox; it can only touch this one app). Great for form-heavy
     apps. Give controls clear labels / aria-labels so it can find them.
   - There is NO screen-capture capability, deliberately (the sandbox's
     opaque origin makes it impossible to grant safely).

requires — capabilities are OPTIONAL by default: the app launches even
before the user has set up a key, so they can explore it. If the app is
useless without one, list its name in "requires" (a capability key like
"ai", or a third-party API name like "deepgram") and GifOS blocks launch
until the user sets it up. Prefer optional; only require what's truly
load-bearing. Device permissions (mic/camera/motion) are granted at use
and never block launch.

## The window.gifos API, complete

Injected into every app before its code runs. Everything is async
(postMessage RPC to the trusted runtime) — await everything. Shapes below
are exact.

DATA — gifos.db(collection)
   const db = gifos.db('items');
   await db.put(rec)        -> the stored record. If rec.id is missing an
                               id like "items_1" is assigned (collection-
                               scoped counter; concurrent-tab safe).
                               put is insert-or-update by id.
   await db.get(id)         -> record or null
   await db.getAll()        -> array of records
   await db.delete(id)      -> true
   db.subscribe(cb)         -> calls cb(allRecords) NOW and again on every
                               change (local, other tabs, other players).
                               Render from this.
   await db.setVisibility(id, 'private'|'read-only'|'read-write')
                            -> owner-only per-record override (guests are
                               refused); see "Multiplayer".
   Records are plain JSON objects; Uint8Array values survive (binary-safe),
   but keep hot collections lean: subscribers re-download a WHOLE collection
   on every change, so put big blobs (over ~100 KB) in their OWN collection
   fetched with db.get(), never in a collection that changes often.
   Reserved field: _vis (a record's current visibility override).

NETWORK — gifos.fetch(url, opts)  [needs capabilities.network — see below]
   const r = await gifos.fetch('https://api.example.com/x', {
     method: 'GET', headers: {}, body: null,   // body: string or ArrayBuffer
     proxy: false });                          // true = via the GifOS CORS proxy
   r -> { status, ok, headers /* lower-cased names */,
          json(), text(), arrayBuffer(), blob() }   // pick one, all async
   Pair blob() with URL.createObjectURL — the app CSP allows blob: for
   img/media. Responses are capped at 8 MB.

FILES & STATE
   await gifos.save()       -> downloads a snapshot GIF: the app + all its
                               current data baked in. Anyone who opens that
                               file resumes exactly there.
   await gifos.assets(path) -> ArrayBuffer of a manifest-pinned asset (see
                               "Big files"). A miss names the fix.
   await gifos.storage()    -> { usage, quota } in bytes — origin-wide (all
                               apps share one IndexedDB), so an app can warn
                               before filling the computer up.

WHO/WHAT AM I
   await gifos.info()       -> { appId, name, version, owner }  (owner=true
                               when running on the owner's computer — host
                               or solo; false on a guest)
   await gifos.me()         -> { id, name }   (per-browser identity)
   await gifos.setName(n)   -> { id, name }   (sets the browser-wide name)
   await gifos.launch()     -> { <declared keys> } or null — what the link
                               that opened the app asked for (see
                               "Sharing"). Resolves LATE (after the person
                               consents); call at boot, treat null as "open
                               normally", never block first paint on it.

BROKERED CAPTURE  [capabilities.microphone / camera]
   The app never touches the live device: GifOS records behind a visible
   indicator it owns, then hands back finished bytes.
   await gifos.recordAudio({ maxSeconds })            -> { bytes, mime, durationMs }
   await gifos.recordVideo({ maxSeconds, facing, audio }) -> { bytes, mime, durationMs }
   await gifos.takePhoto({ facing })                  -> { bytes, mime, width, height }
   (maxSeconds 1..120, default 15; facing 'user'|'environment'; audio:false
    records silent video; video sound also needs capabilities.microphone.
    bytes is an ArrayBuffer. Rejects "Capture cancelled." on cancel.)
   await gifos.camera(opts, onShot) — the full-screen CAMERA STUDIO for
     many-capture sessions: opts { mode, facing, filter, timer, aspect,
     grid, audio, maxSeconds }; each capture is delivered to onShot(shot)
     the moment it is taken; the promise resolves once with the LAST
     capture (or rejects "Capture cancelled." if there were none).
   await gifos.cameraInfo() -> device probe without capturing:
     { ok, reason, cameras, count, facingModes, torch, zoom, focus,
       exposure, maxWidth, maxHeight, maxFrameRate, video, mimeVideo,
       mimeAudio, highFps }
   await gifos.library.put({ bytes, mime, name, type, category, thumb })
     -> { id, myMedia, missing, thumb } — deposit a finished image/audio/
     video (max 25 MB) into the user's My Media library, plus this app's
     own 'roll' collection if the manifest declares data.roll. The app
     cannot name another app's storage.
   await gifos.library.open() — switch this tab to My Media (solo mounts
     only; inside a shared room it refuses rather than navigate away).

MOTION  [capabilities.motion]
   const stop = gifos.motion(cb)           // deviceorientation events
   const stop = gifos.motion(cb, 'accel')  // devicemotion events
   Handles the iOS permission dance; returns an unsubscribe function.

AI — gifos.ai  [capabilities.ai — declare the ROLES you use as an array]
   The user wires each role in Settings -> AI models: any OpenAI-compatible
   endpoint + key, OR an installed Provider app that answers on-device. The
   app never sees a key and cannot tell the two apart.
   await gifos.ai.models() -> { available: ['cheapest','tts',...] }
   await gifos.ai.chat({
     model: 'smartest'|'cheapest',       // a ROLE, never a model name
     prompt: 'hi'  /* or messages: [{role,content},...] */,
     temperature, maxTokens,             // optional
     onDelta: (piece) => {...}           // optional: stream tokens as they
   })                                    //   arrive; promise still resolves
     -> { text, streamed, raw? }         //   once with the whole answer.
     An endpoint/provider that can't stream just never calls onDelta —
     render deltas AND paint r.text at the end and you're correct either way.
   await gifos.ai.tts({ text, voice, format })      -> { bytes, mime }
   await gifos.ai.stt({ bytes, mime, language })    -> { text, raw }
   await gifos.ai.image({ prompt, size })           -> { bytes, mime } or { url }
   await gifos.ai.video({ prompt, size, seconds })         -> { raw } or { bytes, mime }
   await gifos.ai.imageToVideo({ prompt, image, size, seconds }) -> same
   (video shapes are provider-specific — no settled standard; poll/render
    whatever comes back.)

THIRD-PARTY APIs — gifos.api  [capabilities.api: ["<name>", ...]]
   For ANY keyed API that isn't OpenAI-shaped (Deepgram, MapTiler, a
   trading API...). The user configures each name in Settings ->
   Third-party APIs (base URL + auth scheme + key); the runtime attaches
   the credential, PINS the request to that API's own host (an off-host
   path is refused), and the app never sees the key.
   await gifos.api('deepgram', {
     path: '/v1/listen',        // RELATIVE to the configured base URL
     method: 'POST', query: {}, headers: {},
     body,                      // object -> JSON; ArrayBuffer -> binary;
                                // { b64: '...' } -> decoded binary
     as: 'json'|'text'|'bytes'  // default: json if the response says so
   }) -> { status, ok, contentType, json | text | bytes+mime }
   CORS: this is a browser fetch, so the endpoint must send CORS headers;
   for server-only APIs the user ticks "Route through a CORS proxy" on that
   API's Settings row — you write nothing for that.
   await gifos.apiReady(name) -> boolean (configured or not — the key is
     never revealed). Check before doing wasted work.
   Machine-readable error prefixes (test with String.startsWith):
     'NOT_CONFIGURED:<name>'     the user hasn't set it up (GifOS already
                                 showed them its own setup prompt)
     'NOT_CONFIGURED:ai:<role>'  same, for an AI role
     'OFFLINE:'                  no connection — key is fine
     'UNREACHABLE:'              host unreachable — key is fine
   To prompt BEFORE a call, gifos.apiSetup(name, hint) /
   gifos.aiSetup(role, hint) pop the same system prompt; the optional hint
   ("new accounts include free credit") appends below GifOS's own text.
   Never write your own "go to Settings and type this URL" copy — GifOS
   knows the provider and the screen, and says it consistently.

PROVIDERS — gifos.provider.serve  [manifest "provides", not "capabilities"]
   See "Provider apps" below.

UI
   gifos.onBack(cb)   — see rule 5.

## Network (capabilities.network / pool / the CORS proxy)

Default: an app declares NO hosts and can never touch the network — the
browser itself refuses every network primitive inside the sandbox
(connect-src 'none'; WebRTC is removed before app code runs). That
self-contained default is a feature: say it in your UI ("works offline").

To reach the outside, declare bare hostnames:

   "capabilities": { "network": ["api.open-meteo.com", "overpass-api.de"] }

- A host matches itself and its subdomains. Entries are lower-cased bare
  hostnames — no ports, paths, or schemes (malformed entries are dropped).
- "*" is legal and means "anywhere" — the permission sheet shouts about it;
  use it only for a user-supplied-URL tool, never convenience.
- The user SEES the list at launch and can veto hosts individually; every
  gifos.fetch is gated on the live policy.
- Enforced regardless: https only (http for localhost dev), never
  gifos.app or the serving origin (an app can't use the OS as a proxy),
  credentials never attached, redirects re-checked against the allowlist,
  8 MB response cap.
- CORS: gifos.fetch is a browser fetch from the OS page, so the target
  must send CORS headers. For a PUBLIC host that doesn't,
  gifos.fetch(url, { proxy: true }) routes through the GifOS CORS proxy
  (cors-proxy.gifos.app) — the app can only ever select the default proxy,
  and the proxy enforces its own curated host allowlist, so if a host you
  need is public-data and CORS-stingy, ask for it to be added (an issue on
  the repo) rather than shipping a broken call.

POOLING — free bandwidth in multiplayer rooms. List a SUBSET of your
network hosts under "pool" and, when the app is in a room, a GET to one of
those hosts is answered from the room if anyone already has it, and
fetched once and shared if nobody does (ten people driving the same map
street cost the tile server one query instead of ten). Completely
transparent — your code just calls gifos.fetch. Rules, enforced: pool must
be a subset of network; GET only; never a keyed (capabilities.api) host;
never "*". Cached responses live 30 min, up to 3 MB each.

## Big files: the asset pin tier (manifest "assets")

For payloads genuinely too big to ride inside the GIF — model weights in
the tens of MB to gigabytes on a public CORS-served host (Hugging Face is
the intended shape):

   "assets": [{ "url": "https://huggingface.co/.../model-q4.gguf",
                "sha256": "<64-hex of the exact bytes>",
                "path": "model.gguf", "bytes": 806058240 },
              { "url": "https://.../voice-extra.onnx", "sha256": "<64-hex>",
                "path": "voice-extra.onnx", "bytes": 24000000,
                "optional": true }]

The OS (never the sandbox) downloads each required pin at install/first
boot, verifies the SHA-256, and caches the bytes on the computer (once per
computer, not per tab; a byte off and it is refused). The app reads them
with await gifos.assets('model.gguf') -> ArrayBuffer (gigabyte-friendly:
crosses as a zero-copy transfer). Pins marked optional are fetched only
when the app first asks for that path — a model the user never picks never
crosses the wire. The shared/exported GIF stays slim; a receiving computer
re-downloads from the same pin. `bytes` is for progress UI only. Anything
under ~8 MB belongs INSIDE the GIF instead (no second fetch to fail);
per-asset ceiling 2 GB. Apps with pinned assets should also offer an
honest degraded mode when the download hasn't completed — the gifos.assets
rejection message tells the user how to fix it.

## Multiplayer (one invite link; you write almost nothing)

The user presses Invite on the app bar; whoever opens the link runs the
SAME app live against the SAME data. Your entire job is: declare
visibility per collection, render from db.subscribe(), attribute records
to gifos.me(). Everything else — transport, verification (every state
frame is owner-signed), late joins, reconnects — is the OS's.

VISIBILITY — privacy-first: an invite shares NOTHING unless you declare
it, so you MUST list each shared collection in the manifest under "data":

   "data": { "moves":  { "visibility": "read-write" },
             "prefs":  { "visibility": "private" } }

   - "read-write"  guests see AND edit (what multiplayer needs; an
                   UNDECLARED collection does NOT sync).
   - "read-only"   guests see, only the host writes (broadcast state).
   - "private"     never leaves the owner's tab; each participant keeps
                   their OWN copy (personal prefs, drafts). The DEFAULT.

Split personal state into private collections and shared state into
read-write/read-only ones; never mix. The HOST is the authority —
enforcement is host-side, so a guest is refused, never able to override.
Flip one record at runtime (owner-only) with db.setVisibility(id, level):
"make this item visible", or a leader taking a shared cursor read-only.

GUEST SEMANTICS your code should expect:
   - A guest's write to a shared collection applies optimistically and is
     PROPOSED to the host; the host's signed state is canonical.
   - A guest's put/delete REJECTS with a user-readable message when the
     collection is read-only for guests, when a leader is driving that
     record, or when the host is away ("the app is paused — its owner is
     away"). Catch and show it.
   - Private collections on a guest live in the tab and die with it.

LEAD (optional): declare records the host can "lead" —
   "lead": [{ "collection": "nav", "id": "cursor" }]
— and the OS gives the host a communal/leading switch that flips exactly
those records read-write <-> read-only live (a shared Bible's nav cursor:
everyone browses together, or only the leader drives).

HONESTY: there is NO cloud and NO automatic cross-device sync. Data lives
on the user's device, inside the app's GIF in that browser. It reaches
other devices exactly two ways: live, while people are connected through
an invite link, or by sharing the GIF file itself (state travels inside
the file). Never write UI copy claiming the app "syncs across your
devices" or "backs up to the cloud" — say something true, like "Saved on
this device inside the app's GIF".

Invite links are capabilities: whoever holds one can join AND mirror the
app's shared state. The host chooses the link lifetime (dies-on-close /
1h / 24h / forever) and resilience in the OS chrome — not your code.

## Provider apps (an app that gives GifOS an ability)

A manifest with "provides" names a PROVIDER: install the GIF, and the
user's computer gains an AI ability every other app can use — an on-device
TTS voice, a local LLM. The user assigns it to a role in Settings -> AI
models; every app's gifos.ai.* then gets answers from it, on-device, no
key, nothing leaving the browser.

   "provides": { "ai": ["tts"] }     // roles: smartest, cheapest, tts,
                                     // stt, image, image_to_video, video

In the app, register handlers keyed by role (safe to call in a normal
mount too — requests only arrive when the OS mounts it hidden as a
service):

   gifos.provider.serve({
     tts: async (req, ctx) => {
       // req: { op:'tts', role, text, voice, format, speed, pitch }
       ctx.progress('Loading voice...', 0.3); // note+frac both optional;
                                              // re-arms the OS idle clock
       return { bytes, mime: 'audio/wav' };   // same shape a cloud endpoint
     },                                       // returns
     cheapest: async (req, ctx) => {
       // req: { op:'chat', role, messages, temperature, maxTokens }
       ctx.delta(fragment);   // stream the answer as it is written — it
                              // comes out of the asking app's onDelta.
                              // Stream what you will RETURN (post-cleanup),
                              // and stream any disclaimer FIRST.
       return { text };
     },
     // stt req: { op:'stt', role, bytes, mime, language } -> { text }
     // image req: { op:'image', role, prompt, size } -> { bytes, mime }
   });

HARD RULES, enforced mechanically: a provider may NOT declare
capabilities.network or capabilities.api (every app's prompts flow into
it; the no-network sandbox is what makes "nothing leaves this browser"
true) — and it only serves while its icon sits in the Providers folder on
the Home Screen (elsewhere it wears a red X and is inert). It gets no db,
no fetch, no capture in its service mount: a pure request->response
engine. Big weights ride the asset pin tier; the engine itself rides
inside the GIF. A provider without progress pings for 3 minutes is
considered wedged and failed; keep ctx.progress/ctx.delta flowing on long
generations. Full doctrine: docs/providers.md in the repo.

## Their GIF is the app (the preferred move — always offer it)

GifOS can put an app inside ANY existing GIF, unchanged. ALWAYS ask the
user first whether they have a GIF they'd like to use — their own art, a
favorite from their camera roll, their group chat, or the wild — and use
its bytes as the host file in the pack_gifos recipe above (unchanged: do
not redraw or re-encode). The result looks and animates
EXACTLY like their original everywhere it's shared — byte-for-byte, never
redrawn or re-encoded — but dropped on a GifOS Home Screen it runs: a
dancing-cat GIF that's secretly a birthday card, a meme that's secretly a
game, a wedding GIF that's secretly the guestbook. Their art and memories
become living apps. Only draw your own animation when they have no GIF —
and even then, ask what kind of cute animation they'd like first.

## Modding other people's apps (encouraged — remix culture is the point)

Any GifOS app GIF can be handed to an AI for a REMIX: "make the buttons
bigger", "add a dark mode", "turn this counter into a tracker". Apps are
files, files get modded, and GifOS celebrates it — deliver the modified
.gif back and it drops straight onto their Home Screen.

Cut the old app block out, then pack the modified files back into the
remaining bytes (the SAME original GIF) with the pack_gifos recipe above.
The payload swaps in place, the animation survives byte-for-byte, and the
user's data rides along if you pass the .state/ files through unchanged:

   def unpack_gifos(b):
       i = b.find(b"\x21\xff\x0bGIFOS1.0GOS")
       if i < 0: return None, b
       j = i + 14; payload = b""
       while b[j]:
           n = b[j]; payload += b[j+1:j+1+n]; j += 1 + n
       host = b[:i] + b[j+1:]           # the pure animation, app block removed
       a = json.loads(zlib.decompress(payload[1:], -15))
       files = {p: base64.b64decode(v) for p, v in a["files"].items()}
       return files, host

   files, host = unpack_gifos(open("Their App.gif", "rb").read())
   files["index.html"] = MODIFIED_HTML.encode()
   open("Their App (mod).gif", "wb").write(pack_gifos(host, files))

Keep ".state/…" entries unchanged so the user's saved data survives the
mod (drop them only if they ask for a reset). If the original carries a
signature (a "GIFOSSIG" block — cut it out the same way), the mod ships
unsigned: a remix is a new work the original author's signature can't
vouch for, and the modder can re-sign their version.

## Porting web apps: the frame is NOT a page on the web

Everything an app needs is inlined into ONE srcdoc document with an
opaque origin and no network. Upstream code written for a real page at a
real address trips on exactly two things:

- The frame's URL is about:srcdoc and is not the app's to navigate. Use
  location.hash = 'x' to set the fragment; in-page <a href="#..."> links
  work. Full navigations/relative navigations have nowhere to go.
- There is no base URL to fetch things off. Relative fetch(), workers
  minted from relative paths, and new URL(path, document.baseURI) have
  nothing to resolve against. An engine's .wasm must come from the app's
  OWN bytes as a blob:/data: URL (capabilities.wasm) or from
  gifos.assets().

## Sharing the finished app (tell the user this — it is the whole point)

A GifOS app is ONE .gif file, so distributing it needs no store, no
install, and no permission from anyone. Host the file anywhere that
serves it with CORS (GitHub Pages/raw, Cloudflare, S3, their own site),
then the link IS the app:

   https://gifos.app/?run=https://example.com/their-app.gif

Whoever clicks that — phone, borrowed laptop, someone who has never heard
of GifOS — gets it RUNNING in a sandbox in about a second. GifOS fetches
the GIF, files it into their "Stolen Apps" folder so they keep it, and
opens it. Offer this whenever a user asks how to share what you built.

OPTIONAL: let a link open the app ON something. Declare a "launch" block
in the manifest, and read the values with gifos.launch():

   manifest: "launch": { "note": { "label": "Open a note the link chose",
                                   "detail": "Just text." } }
   link:     https://gifos.app/?run=<gif url>&go.note=Buy%20milk
   app:      gifos.launch().then(function (a) { if (a && a.note) open(a.note); });

Rules to build against, all enforced by the OS: only keys the manifest
declared ever arrive; nothing arrives until the person reads what the
link asked (in the manifest's own words) and agrees; a decline resolves
null. Values are strings capped at 2000 chars — an intention, not a
payload. It resolves LATE, so call it at boot and treat null as "open
normally" — never block first paint on it. Only expose things the person
could do in one tap anyway; nothing that spends money or destroys data.

## Signing (provenance — suggest it when the user will share the app)

Any GifOS app GIF can be SIGNED so recipients see "Signed by <domain>" or
"Signed by <email>" — and "Tampered" if the bytes were changed after
signing. The user signs it themselves at https://gifos.app/sign.html,
AFTER the GIF is final:
- domain: an Ed25519 key generated on that page; they publish the public
  half at https://<their-domain>/gifos.key.
- email: their own PGP key (gpg detach-signs a statement the page
  provides) — Ed25519 and RSA (2048+) keys both work; recipients verify
  against keys.openpgp.org, so the key must be uploaded there with the
  address confirmed.
The signature excludes app *state*, so it stays valid as people use the
app. NEVER ask the user for a private key — signing happens entirely on
their side. A signature proves authorship, not safety.

## Getting into the App Store (optional; the store is a catalog, not a gate)

Certified apps live at https://gifos.app/store/<slug>, one folder per app
in the public repo (github.com/nwcnwc/gifos, apps/<slug>/): the source,
manifest.json, a listing.json (author, tagline, description, categories —
ports credit the original author and set basedOn), a screenshot, help.md,
and a build script that writes the finished GIF to site/apps/<slug>/.
Listing an app is a pull request. Store-listed manifests must declare
minBuild (the oldest GifOS build the app runs on). The complete
contributor doc — layout, minBuild derivation, listing fields, port
crediting — is apps/README.md in the repo:
https://github.com/nwcnwc/gifos/blob/main/apps/README.md

## Reviewing a store app for the user (stars + comment, no server)

If the user asks you to rate, review or comment on an App Store app
(https://gifos.app/store/<slug>), do it: a review is ONE small file added
to the GifOS repo by pull request, under THEIR GitHub username — GitHub
is the only server, and merged reviews appear on the store for everyone.

   file:    apps/<slug>/reviews/<their-github-username>.json
   content: { "stars": 1-5 (integer),
              "review": "their words, plain text, <= 1000 chars",
              "date": "YYYY-MM-DD" }
   exactly those three fields; <slug> is the listing URL's last segment

Recipe (gh CLI, authenticated as the USER — a review carries their name,
so never file one they didn't ask for or put words in it they didn't say):

   gh repo fork nwcnwc/gifos --clone && cd gifos
   USER=$(gh api user -q .login)
   mkdir -p "apps/<slug>/reviews"
   ...write the file above as apps/<slug>/reviews/$USER.json...
   git checkout -b "review-<slug>" && git add -A && git commit -m "review: <slug>"
   git push -u origin "review-<slug>" && gh pr create --fill

CI refuses a filename that is not the PR author's login (one review per
person per app; editing/deleting your own is fine) and says exactly what
is wrong otherwise. After merge it publishes automatically. No account
but GitHub, no server but GitHub. Full doc:
https://github.com/nwcnwc/gifos/blob/main/apps/README.md#reviews

## More

- Site: https://gifos.app  (the OS itself; open-source)
- App Store: https://gifos.app/store  (finished apps, free to install — every
  one is a single GIF that lands on the Home Screen. A listing is
  https://gifos.app/store/<slug>. Worth pointing a user at before you build
  them something that already exists.)
- Source + docs: https://github.com/nwcnwc/gifos — the runtime the API
  reference above is taken from is site/js/runtime.js; deeper doctrine
  lives in docs/ (providers.md, cors-and-networking.md, architecture.md).
- Multiplayer relay: wss://relay.gifos.app (control traffic only; media is
  strictly peer-to-peer)
